heading: M1-Q46 (V2-D5.3)
question:
A contract-signing agent prepares signature packets. A wrong signature binds the company to bad terms.

Which review shape fits?

choices.B: Do a pre-action approval. A qualified signer reviews the exact packet and terms. This happens before any signing.
choices.C: Do not do a review. The agent is accurate.

explanation: Decisive phrase: "A wrong signature binds the company to bad terms." Why: signing is irreversible and high-consequence. Only pre-action approval with full context can stop the harm. A reviews after binding. Counterfactual: A wins for reversible low-stakes packets.

heading: M1-Q47 (V2-D5.3)
question:
A drafting agent writes internal status updates. Volume is 2,000 per day. Stakes are low and everything is reversible.

Which review shape fits?

choices.B: Sampled human review plus audit logging.

explanation: Decisive phrase: "2,000 per day. Stakes are low and everything is reversible." Why: pre-action approval at this volume becomes rubber-stamp theater. Sampled review plus complete logs give real detection cheaply. Counterfactual: A wins at 20 drafts per day with high stakes.

heading: M1-Q48 (V2-D5.4), Select TWO
question:
A health chatbot handles patient messages. HIPAA applies. The team has access controls but no named owner and no review schedule.

Which TWO links complete the compliance chain? Select TWO.

choices.A: A named owner for the access controls.
choices.B: A review cadence: re-check the controls on a schedule.

explanation: Decisive phrase: "no named owner and no review schedule." Why: the chain is requirement to control to owner to evidence to cadence. Name the missing links explicitly. C, D, and E are not chain links. Counterfactual: none. Cosmetics never complete compliance.

heading: M1-Q49 (V2-D5.4)
question:
A support bot stores EU customer tickets. The team sets retention: tickets auto-delete after 3 years, sooner on customer request.

What makes this retention design sound?

choices.B: The retention rule tied to the requirement, with an owner, evidence of enforcement, and a review cadence. Plus the on-request deletion path.

explanation:
Decisive phrase: "auto-delete after 3 years, sooner on customer request." Why: retention is a link in the compliance chain: requirement, control, owner, evidence, cadence. The deletion path honors the request right. C destroys business evidence. D ignores the requirement.

Counterfactual: C wins only if a rule truly demands one-day deletion.

heading: M1-Q50 (V2-D5.5)
question:
A loan assistant denies applications. Applicants ask why.

What does responsible AI require?

choices.B: Traceability: Link the decision to the factors and data. Explain the decision to the applicant. Measure per-group fairness.

explanation:
The decisive phrase is "Applicants ask why." V2-D5.5 requires transparency. It requires explainability. It requires accountability. It requires traceability. The decision must link to its factors.

Measure fairness per group. A and D give up responsibility. Opacity is never the answer.

heading: M1-Q51 (V2-D6.1)
question:
A warehouse wants a picking assistant that is "accurate and fast." Volume is 5,000 picks per day. Errors ship wrong products.

What is the first discovery output?

choices.B: These are measurable requirements. "Accurate" means pick accuracy is 99.5% or more. "Fast" means p95 pick time is less than 20 seconds. Record the error cost and the volume.

explanation: The decisive phrase is "'accurate and fast'... Errors ship wrong products." Discovery changes adjectives to numbers before any build. A, C, and D use adjectives. A wins after the team signs the requirements.

heading: M1-Q52 (V2-D6.1), Select TWO
question:
A discovery session for a claims bot ends with: volume unknown, compliance needs unknown, the data source "probably the warehouse."

Select the TWO open assumptions to record.
explanation:
Decisive phrase: "volume unknown, compliance needs unknown, the data source 'probably.'" Why: V2-D6.1 records open assumptions explicitly with owners. Volume and compliance shape the whole design. C, D, and E are irrelevant. Counterfactual: none.

Trivia is never a discovery output.

heading: M1-Q53 (V2-D6.2)
question:
An architect proposes a new vendor for document storage. Legal asks about the trade-off.

What does legal need to hear?

choices.B: Compliance impact, data residency, contract risk, reversal cost, and audit evidence per option.

explanation: Decisive phrase: "Legal asks about the trade-off." Why: V2-D6.2 adapts benefit, cost, risk, reversal cost, and compliance impact to the audience. Legal decides on exactly these axes. Counterfactual: A wins for the CFO's first slide, never alone for legal.

heading: M1-Q54 (V2-D6.2)
question:
A team debates switching vector databases. The current one holds 40M vectors with custom metadata.

Which trade-off axis matters most here?

choices.B: Reversal and migration cost: re-indexing 40M vectors, metadata mapping, dual-run period, and rollback plan.

explanation: Decisive phrase: "holds 40M vectors with custom metadata." Why: migration cost dominates the decision at this scale. V2-D6.2 requires reversal cost per option. The rest are trivia. Counterfactual: D wins never as a decision axis.

heading: M1-Q55 (V2-D6.3), Select TWO
question:
A team ships a triage bot to the CIO with the promise "the AI handles it."

Which TWO make the handoff honest? Select TWO.

choices.A: Measured quality per ticket class with the eval date.
choices.B: Review triggers and breach consequences: what happens when quality drops or a new class appears.
choices.C: "The AI handles it" as the SLA.

explanation: Decisive phrase: "'the AI handles it.'" Why: honest handoff needs measurable quality and named triggers with consequences. C, D, and E are slogans or silence. Counterfactual: none. Slogans are never SLA terms.
